framework_name: AI Operating Model (CoE vs Hub-and-Spoke vs Federated)
creator_or_source: Composite framework synthesized from multiple sources: Harvard Business Review (Tim Fountaine, Brian McCarthy, Tamim Saleh, 2019), Dataiku (Conor Jensen, 2025), McKinsey & Company, AWS, and various enterprise consulting practices. Not a single-author framework but an industry-standard taxonomy for organizing AI teams within enterprises.
year_introduced: 2019 (HBR 'Building the AI-Powered Organization' formalized the hub-and-spoke model; the taxonomy has evolved through 2024-2025 with additions like 'Center for Acceleration' and 'Embedded' models)
scope: Team design, Governance, Full project lifecycle
key_components:
The framework defines 4-5 organizational models for structuring AI teams in enterprises, typically presented as a maturity progression:

1. **Siloed Model**: Each team does independent AI experimentation with no shared infrastructure, data, or best practices. This is the starting point for most companies — the goal is to figure out if AI is worth further investment. Almost always temporary (a few quarters to a couple of years).

2. **Center of Excellence (CoE) / Centralized Model**: A single centralized team of AI specialists develops and maintains AI products for all business units. Key tasks include: managing a portfolio of AI products and prioritizing a backlog, creating scalable data architecture, tracking AI industry innovation, developing champions in each business unit, and capturing and evangelizing AI value stories. Strengths: uniform governance, consistent standards, fast jumpstart. Weaknesses: bottlenecks, slower responsiveness, maintenance costs grow as portfolio expands. Real-world examples: JPMorgan Chase (MLCoE for AML models), Walmart (cross-functional AI CoE), Siemens (central AI Lab).

3. **Hub-and-Spoke Model**: AI experts remain in a central hub while business units form the spokes. Unlike the CoE where communication is mainly via product requests, in hub-and-spoke they collaborate directly on product development. The hub handles infrastructure, standards, and industry innovation tracking. Product ownership shifts to the spokes — they prioritize the backlog, drive adoption, track performance, and are responsible for generating value. Companies that have scaled AI are 3x more likely to use this structure (HBR, 2019). Strengths: balances governance with domain proximity, reduces isolation of data teams from business. Weaknesses: requires clear role definition, resourcing challenges, cultural alignment. Real-world examples: Meta/Facebook (central data engineering + autonomous product teams), Mastercard (centralized AI leadership + decentralized execution).

4. **Center for Acceleration**: A refinement of hub-and-spoke, recommended by Dataiku for organizations with mature CoEs. Shifts the onus for AI product development into business units, aiming to create 'unicorn teams' (multidisciplinary AI-capable teams) in every spoke. The center focuses on training, platform management, responsible AI guidelines, and knowledge sharing rather than building products. Strengths: increased innovation (domain experts participate), increased agility, higher ROI since business units invest their own effort. Weaknesses: requires high AI maturity across the organization.

5. **Embedded / Fully Decentralized Model**: Very few central shared resources — just responsible AI guidelines, infrastructure, and common datasets. Each business unit has full ownership of its AI capabilities. Represents the most decentralized, agile, and innovative structure. Real-world examples: Booking.com (data scientists embedded directly in product teams), Amazon, Google, Uber (digital natives that have always embedded data science). Strengths: maximum agility and domain knowledge. Weaknesses: fragmented tools, duplicated efforts, governance drift, poor scalability without strong coordination.

The models are typically presented as a maturity progression: Siloed → CoE → Hub-and-Spoke → Center for Acceleration → Embedded, though organizations may skip stages or adopt hybrid variants depending on their context.
typical_use_case: An enterprise leader deciding how to structure their AI organization. Typical scenario: a company has run successful AI pilots in isolated teams (siloed stage) and now wants to scale AI across the organization. They use this framework to evaluate whether to centralize AI talent in a CoE for governance and rapid capability building, adopt a hub-and-spoke model to balance central standards with business-unit autonomy, or move toward an embedded model for maximum agility. The framework is also used when selling AI services or consulting to enterprises — understanding which operating model a client uses determines how to position products and engagement models.
deliverables: Organizational design recommendation, governance structure, role definitions, transition roadmap (phased timeline from centralized to federated), KPIs for measuring AI team effectiveness (ROI, time to market, adoption rate, number of AI products per business unit)
genai_relevance: High — The framework has been actively updated for the GenAI era (2024-2025). AWS published a dedicated guide on GenAI operating models (centralized, decentralized, federated) in January 2025 specifically for Amazon Bedrock deployments. The federated model is particularly relevant for GenAI because it allows business units to experiment rapidly with LLM use cases while central teams manage guardrails, model risk management, data privacy, and compliance. McKinsey's 2025 'Agentic Organization' concept further evolves this toward AI-first workflow design. The Center for Acceleration model explicitly addresses scaling GenAI and AI agent development practices across both data scientists and business analysts.
accessibility_for_non_engineers: High — The framework is fundamentally an organizational and management concept, not a technical one. Business students can readily understand the trade-offs between centralized control and decentralized agility using everyday analogies: Centralized = Air Traffic Control Tower (one central tower coordinates all movements), Federated = Local Airport Towers (each airport manages traffic locally), Hybrid = Both (central HQ for major routes, local towers for day-to-day). The framework is commonly presented with simple diagrams showing hub-spoke relationships. No coding or technical knowledge required to understand or discuss the models.
time_to_apply: Multi-week assessment for initial evaluation; ongoing process for implementation. Phase 1 (0-12 months): establish centralized CoE with governance and shared stack. Phase 2 (12-24 months): evolve to hybrid hub-and-spoke with AI champions in business units. Phase 3 (24-36 months): mature into federated pods with high autonomy. Full organizational transformation typically takes 2-3 years.
free_or_paid: Free — The core concepts are publicly available through HBR articles, AWS blogs, Dataiku blogs, McKinsey publications, and numerous consulting firm whitepapers. No paid tools required to understand or apply the framework, though implementation may benefit from consulting engagement.
adoption_level: Industry standard — Hub-and-spoke is the 2025 consensus model for scaled AI organizations. The HBR research found that companies that have scaled AI are 3x more likely than average to use a hub-and-spoke structure. The International Institute for Analytics identified hub-and-spoke as the most popular model among enterprise leaders. Major enterprises (JPMorgan, Walmart, Siemens, Meta, Uber, Airbnb, Mastercard, Booking.com, Spotify) have publicly documented their adoption of variants of these models.
ai_project_stage: Multiple — The framework applies across all stages but is most critical at the Scale stage when organizations move from successful pilots to enterprise-wide AI deployment. The Siloed model serves Ideation/PoC, CoE serves PoC/MVP, Hub-and-Spoke serves Production/Scale, and Embedded serves Scale/Maintenance.
relevance_for_entrepreneurs: Critical for two reasons: (1) If you are building an AI startup selling to enterprises, you must understand your client's AI operating model to know who your buyer is, how decisions get made, and where your product fits. Selling to a centralized CoE is very different from selling to federated business units. (2) If you are scaling your own startup's AI capabilities, you need to decide when to centralize vs. embed AI talent. Most startups start embedded (small teams, everyone does everything), but as they grow, they face the same organizational design decisions as large enterprises. Understanding the maturity progression helps founders plan their team structure proactively rather than reactively.
complements: Pairs well with: CRISP-DM (provides the project lifecycle that operates within whatever operating model is chosen), AI Canvas (helps individual teams within any operating model structure their projects), AI Maturity Models (provides the assessment that determines which operating model stage an organization should target), Build vs Buy Decision Framework (the operating model influences whether to build or buy — centralized CoEs tend to build more, embedded models tend to buy more platform tools).
limitations: 1. The framework presents models as a clean progression, but real organizations often operate in messy hybrids that don't fit neatly into one category. 2. The '3x more likely' hub-and-spoke statistic is from 2019 research and predates the GenAI era; the landscape is evolving rapidly with agentic AI. 3. The framework focuses on large enterprises — startups and SMEs may find the CoE/hub-and-spoke models over-engineered for their scale. 4. Cultural and organizational politics are underemphasized — transitioning from centralized to federated requires significant change management that the framework acknowledges but doesn't deeply address. 5. Geographic and regulatory differences (e.g., EU AI Act compliance requirements) may force different structural choices than the maturity model suggests. 6. The framework doesn't adequately address the 'right-sizing' question — how large should the central hub actually be relative to the spokes?
example_application: Scenario: A European fintech startup with 50 employees has grown from 3 to 15 people working on AI/ML across fraud detection, credit scoring, and customer service chatbots. Currently siloed — each product team has its own data scientist working independently. The CEO uses this framework to design the next stage: they establish a small central AI hub (3 people) responsible for shared ML infrastructure (feature store, model registry, monitoring), data governance and EU AI Act compliance, and maintaining coding standards. The remaining 12 AI practitioners stay embedded in their product teams (spokes) but now use shared infrastructure and follow central governance. This hub-and-spoke model lets the startup maintain speed of innovation in each product area while ensuring regulatory compliance and avoiding duplicated infrastructure work.
available_templates: No single canonical template exists, but several resources provide practical tools: Dataiku's 'Align Your Operating Model With Your AI Maturity' guide (https://blog.dataiku.com/align-your-operating-model-with-your-ai-maturity), AWS GenAI Operating Model architectures with detailed AWS account structure diagrams (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/generative-ai-operating-models-in-enterprise-organizations-with-amazon-bedrock/), Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework AI CoE guide (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/scenarios/ai/center-of-excellence), Zinnov's 4 Pillars of AI CoE blueprint (https://zinnov.com/centers-of-excellence/the-4-pillars-of-ai-coes-a-blueprint-for-enterprise-scale-ai-blog/).
regulatory_alignment: EU AI Act (the federated model with central governance is well-suited for EU AI Act compliance — central team manages risk classification, conformity assessments, and documentation while business units handle domain-specific implementation), GDPR (federated models allow sensitive data to remain in business-unit-controlled environments), NIST AI RMF (the governance structures in hub-and-spoke models map well to NIST AI RMF organizational governance functions), ISO 42001 (the centralized governance component of hub-and-spoke models supports ISO 42001 AI management system requirements)
